title: The Secret of the Brass Heron

passage.title: The Secret of the Brass Heron
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Every Saturday morning, Leo climbed the narrow wooden stairs to his Uncle Mateo's clock shop near the Savannah riverfront. Hundreds of ticking pendulums filled the warm room with a steady pulse. Most kids spent their weekends at the soccer field. Leo preferred sorting tiny brass gears at the corner workbench. This morning, a tall clock shaped like a marsh heron stood beside his lamp. Its tarnished wings were folded tight against its sides. Its long beak pointed down toward the silent dial.

Uncle Mateo set a leather tool roll on the desk. He tapped the bird's metal shoulder with a smile. For thirty years, the clock had sat untouched in a coastal attic after salt air froze its springs. Using slender brass tweezers, Leo lifted the faceplate to inspect the dark space behind the numerals. The rusted balance wheel, jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand, was gently freed by Leo with a soft horsehair brush. As the last speck of grit fell away, he spotted a silver lever beneath the main gear.

At first, Leo felt reluctant to press the strange lever without asking his uncle for help. A careless push could snap a fragile tooth and ruin a week of patient repair work. Instead of forcing the part, he traced the lever's path with his flashlight beam until he understood how the rods connected. The silver arm bypassed the hour bell completely. It linked straight to a hinged joint inside the heron's neck. When Leo nudged the catch with steady fingers, a hidden spring unwound with a low, musical whirr.

Across the room, Uncle Mateo looked up from his bench with wide eyes. The brass heron was coming alive. The bird slowly dipped its slender head toward the base as if plucking a minnow from shallow water. Then its wings spread an inch apart, revealing a miniature painted scene of Tybee Lighthouse glowing behind glass. None of the modern clocks in the front window held such a clever surprise inside their cases. The builder had crafted a work of art meant only for someone patient enough to clean every gear.

Uncle Mateo walked over and placed a proud hand on Leo's shoulder. The brass wings folded shut again with a soft click. He noted that impatient workers often swapped old gears for cheap battery boxes instead of cleaning the original parts. By respecting the old craft and looking closely before acting, Leo had saved the clock's rarest feature from being lost forever. Leo smiled and reached for his cloth, eager to make the brass feathers shine like new.

tier2Words.definition: dull or discolored from exposure to air and moisture over time
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French ternir, meaning 'to make dim or dull'

tier2Words.definition: to look at something closely and carefully in order to check its condition
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root spect- ('to look') + prefix in- ('into')
tier2Words.contextClue: Leo lifted the faceplate to look into the dark space behind the numerals.

tier2Words.definition: hesitant and unwilling to do something right away because of caution
tier2Words.contextClue: Leo hesitated to press the strange lever because a careless push could snap a fragile tooth.

tier2Words.definition: built or painted on a very small scale compared to full size
tier2Words.rootHint: From Italian miniatura, referring to tiny detailed book illustrations
tier2Words.contextClue: The tiny painted scene of Tybee Lighthouse fit inside the clock case behind the heron's wings.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The rusted balance wheel, jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand, was gently freed by Leo with a soft horsehair brush."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what caused the balance wheel to stop moving in the first place, and who freed it?

options.text: Leo jammed the balance wheel with a horsehair brush, and Uncle Mateo freed it using dried oil.
options.childFeedback: This flips the actions backward! Paragraph 2 says Leo used the soft horsehair brush to free the wheel, not jam it, and Uncle Mateo did not use dried oil.

options.text: Dried oil and marsh sand jammed the balance wheel, and Leo freed it using a horsehair brush.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand' shows what stopped the wheel, and 'freed by Leo' shows who fixed it.

options.text: A soft horsehair brush jammed the tiny grains of sand until the balance wheel freed itself.
options.childFeedback: A brush cannot jam sand so a wheel frees itself! Paragraph 2 says Leo used the horsehair brush to gently brush the grit away and free the wheel.

options.text: Salt water from a hurricane flooded the entire clock shop and rusted the silver chime lever.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 never mentions a hurricane flooding the clock shop; it says the clock sat in a coastal attic for thirty years where salt air and sand jammed it.

questions.provingSentenceText: The rusted balance wheel, jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand, was gently freed by Leo with a soft horsehair brush.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand' shows what stopped the wheel, and 'freed by Leo' shows who fixed it.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive-voice sentence contains two 'by' prepositional phrases: 'jammed by decades of dried oil and tiny grains of marsh sand' (the cause of the jam) and 'was gently freed by Leo' (the actor who fixed it). Option B accurately tracks both agents, while Option A reverses the actors.
questions.retryHint: Reread the long sentence in Paragraph 2 and look for the words 'jammed by' and 'freed by' to see who did each action.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 3:

"At first, Leo felt reluctant to press the strange lever without asking his uncle for help. A careless push could snap a fragile tooth and ruin a week of patient repair work."

What does the word reluctant mean as it is used in Paragraph 3?

options.text: Excited and eager to test a new tool right away
options.childFeedback: This is the opposite of what happened! Paragraph 3 says Leo held back from pressing the lever right away because a careless push could break a gear.

options.text: Completely unable to see inside the dark clock case
options.childFeedback: Leo could see inside the clock just fine with his flashlight beam; he paused because he didn't want to break a fragile part by pushing too fast.

options.text: Hesitant and cautious about acting too quickly
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'reluctant' means hesitant and cautious, because Leo worried that a careless push on the lever might snap a fragile gear tooth.

options.text: Angry that his uncle gave him a broken antique clock
options.childFeedback: Leo was not angry at his uncle at all! Paragraph 1 and Paragraph 3 show he loved fixing clocks and wanted to protect his careful repair work.

questions.provingSentenceText: At first, Leo felt reluctant to press the strange lever without asking his uncle for help.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'reluctant' means hesitant and cautious, because Leo worried that a careless push on the lever might snap a fragile gear tooth.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3, the sentence immediately following 'reluctant' explains Leo's caution ('A careless push could snap a fragile tooth'). Option C captures this careful hesitation.
questions.retryHint: Read the very next sentence in Paragraph 3 to see what Leo worried might happen if he pushed the lever too carelessly.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why does Leo shine his flashlight along the silver lever before touching it?

options.text: He wants to understand how the hidden parts connect so he does not damage the clock.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that Leo traced the lever's path with his flashlight to see how the rods connected before nudging it, protecting the fragile gears.

options.text: He is looking for a place to install a modern battery box inside the heron's neck.
options.childFeedback: Leo wasn't installing a battery box! Paragraph 5 explains that impatient workers used cheap battery boxes, while Leo carefully cleaned the original gears.

options.text: He never touches any clock in the shop unless Uncle Mateo holds the flashlight for him.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 shows Leo using the flashlight and nudging the catch by himself while Uncle Mateo was working across the room at his own bench.

options.text: He hopes to find gold coins that the original owner hid behind the clock numerals.
options.childFeedback: The story never says anything about hidden gold coins; Leo was tracing how the silver lever connected to the hinged joint in the heron's neck.

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead of forcing the part, he traced the lever's path with his flashlight beam until he understood how the rods connected.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that Leo traced the lever's path with his flashlight to see how the rods connected before nudging it, protecting the fragile gears.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 states that instead of forcing the lever and risking a broken gear tooth, Leo traced its path with his flashlight until he understood how the rods connected (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Check Paragraph 3 right after Leo worries about snapping a tooth to see what he uses his flashlight beam to figure out.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 4 contribute to the overall structure of the story?

options.text: It introduces the setting of the Savannah clock shop and explains why Leo dislikes soccer.
options.childFeedback: The Savannah clock shop setting and Leo's preference for gears over soccer are introduced back in Paragraph 1, not Paragraph 4.

options.text: It proves that modern clocks in store windows are always more reliable than antique clocks.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 actually says the opposite: none of the modern clocks in the front window held such a clever artistic surprise inside their cases.

options.text: It explains how salt air along the Georgia coast causes brass springs to freeze over time.
options.childFeedback: How salt air froze the springs in a coastal attic is background information explained in Paragraph 2, whereas Paragraph 4 shows the bird coming alive.

options.text: It reveals the climax of Leo's discovery by showing what the hidden mechanism does when triggered.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 is the exciting turning point of the story where the brass heron dips its head and opens its wings to reveal the glowing Tybee Lighthouse scene.

questions.provingSentenceText: Then its wings spread an inch apart, revealing a miniature painted scene of Tybee Lighthouse glowing behind glass.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 is the exciting turning point of the story where the brass heron dips its head and opens its wings to reveal the glowing Tybee Lighthouse scene.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 serves as the story's turning point/climax where Leo's careful cleaning and observation pay off as the heron dips its head and spreads its wings to reveal the miniature Tybee Lighthouse scene.
questions.retryHint: Read Paragraph 4 to see the surprising moment that happens right after Leo nudges the hidden silver catch.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central theme of the story?

options.text: Ten-year-old apprentices cannot repair delicate machines without constant help from an adult.
options.childFeedback: Leo actually repairs the clock and unlocks the hidden mechanism on his own while Uncle Mateo watches proudly from across the shop.

options.text: Antique clocks kept near the ocean should always be converted to battery power so they do not rust.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says the exact opposite: swapping old gears for cheap battery boxes would have destroyed the clock's rarest hidden feature forever.

options.text: Patient care and close observation can uncover hidden beauty that rushed shortcuts would destroy.
options.childFeedback: Across the story, Leo's patient cleaning and careful observation unlock the heron's hidden lighthouse scene, which a rushed battery swap would have ruined.

options.text: A horsehair brush is the most important tool on a clockmaker's workbench.
options.childFeedback: The horsehair brush is just one small tool Leo uses in Paragraph 2, not the big life lesson of the whole story.

questions.provingSentenceText: By respecting the old craft and looking closely before acting, Leo had saved the clock's rarest feature from being lost forever.
questions.childTip: Across the story, Leo's patient cleaning and careful observation unlock the heron's hidden lighthouse scene, which a rushed battery swap would have ruined.
questions.parentExplanation: The central theme (ELAGSE5RL2) contrasts impatient shortcuts (replacing movements with battery boxes or forcing levers) with Leo's patient cleaning and close observation, which preserved the clock's hidden artwork.
questions.retryHint: Look at Paragraph 5 to see what Uncle Mateo says Leo's patience saved compared to what impatient workers usually do.

options.text: "Every Saturday morning, Leo climbed the narrow wooden stairs to his Uncle Mateo's clock shop near the Savannah riverfront."
